faq.a: Decomposers are living things, mainly bacteria and fungi, that feed on dead plants and animals and break them down into simple chemicals.

faq.q: Why does rotting food smell bad?
faq.a: As decomposers break down proteins, they release smelly gases such as hydrogen sulfide, which smells of rotten eggs, and ammonia. The smell warns animals away.
asks: What is the smell of rotting?

faq.q: Why does a compost heap get warm?
faq.a: Millions of microbes are busy breaking down the waste, and like us they give off heat as they use food. A busy heap can reach about 60 degrees Celsius.

faq.q: Why does food rot slower in the fridge?
faq.a: Decomposers grow and work much more slowly in the cold, so food stays fresh for longer.
asks: How does a fridge stop food going off?

faq.q: Why don't things rot in very dry or very cold places?
faq.a: Decomposers need water and warmth. In deserts, ice or very salty places they cannot work, which is why mummies and frozen mammoths have survived for thousands of years.

facts: A busy compost heap can heat up to around 60 degrees Celsius from the work of microbes.
Rotting returns carbon to the air as carbon dioxide, as part of the carbon cycle.

quiz.say: Why does a freezer stop food from rotting?
quiz.show: Why does a freezer stop food from rotting?

options.show: Cold kills every germ for ever
options.say: Cold kills every germ for ever

quiz.why: Decomposers need warmth to grow and work, so freezing pauses rotting.

wrong.0: Many microbes survive freezing and become active again when food thaws.
wrong.1: Frozen food keeps its nutrients; the microbes just cannot use them.
